To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the activity of CFTR is required for deformation of RBC-induced ATP release from both human and rabbit RBCs.
mechanical stimulation of RBCs results in the release of ATP and that this process requires CFTR activity.
mechanical deformation of RBC releases ATP, and this ATP release is inhibited in the presence of CFTR inhibitors or in CF patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the CFTR in the release of ATP from red blood cells (erythrocytes) and in the control of vascular resistance.
the hypothesis that the cystic fibro-transmembrane conductance channel (CFTR) is required for ATP release from red cells in response to mechanical strain.
the regulation of vascular tone and the role that the cystic fibrotic transmembrane conductase regulator (CFTR) plays in the release of ATP from red blood cells (rbc).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CFTR channel is a necessary but not sufficient condition for deformation-induced ATP secretion from human RBC.
CFTR activity is required for ATP release from Rbc's in response to mechanical strain.
the ATP released in response to mechanical stimulation is likely to be a paracrine regulator of vascular tone and blood flow.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CFTR is required for ATP release from RBDs.
CFTR is involved in the regulation of ATP release from RBSs.
CFTR activity in red blood cells is required for the release of ATP in response to cell deformation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CFTR plays a critical role in the regulation of the release of ATP from RBCs in response to mechanical stimuli.
the ATP released by RBCs in response to deformation may play a role in the regulation of blood flow and blood pressure.
CFTR is involved in ATP release from red cells in response to mechanical stress.
